content: Yellow fever is a severe illness caused by the yellow fever virus. Most individuals infected with the virus either remain asymptomatic or experience only mild symptoms. However, for those who do develop symptoms, these typically appear 3 to 6 days after infection and may include fever, chills, headache, backache, and muscle aches. Approximately 12% of symptomatic individuals progress to a more severe form of the disease, which can involve jaundice, bleeding, shock, organ failure, and, in some cases, death. The yellow fever virus is transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes. The virus and the mosquitoes that carry it are primarily found in specific regions of South America and Africa. Travelers to these areas are at risk of contracting the virus. It is essential to check whether the yellow fever vaccine is recommended or required for your travel destination. Some countries mandate proof of vaccination for entry as a public health safeguard to prevent the importation of the virus. This proof is provided through the International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis (ICVP), also known as the yellow card. Travelers should plan to receive the vaccine at least 10 days before departure, as it takes this amount of time for immunity to develop, and the certificate becomes valid only after this period. A single dose of the vaccine typically provides lifelong protection, though a booster dose may be recommended for certain individuals after 10 years. It is important to consult with a healthcare provider to determine if vaccination is necessary for your travel plans and to discuss any potential risks, especially for individuals over 60 years old, those with weakened immune systems, or pregnant and nursing women. Use an EPA-registered insect repellent containing active ingredients such as picaridin, oil of lemon eucalyptus (OLE), or para-menthane-diol (PMD). When applying both sunscreen and insect repellent, always apply the repellent after the sunscreen. For children, dress them in clothing that covers their arms and legs, use mosquito netting over strollers and carriers, and avoid applying repellent to their hands, eyes, mouth, or irritated skin. Products containing OLE or PMD should not be used on children under 3 years old. Treat clothing and gear with 0.5% permethrin, an insecticide that repels and kills mosquitoes. Permethrin-treated clothing remains effective after multiple washes, but it should never be applied directly to the skin. Follow product instructions carefully when treating items yourself. To keep mosquitoes out of your accommodations, choose lodging with air conditioning or window and door screens. If these are unavailable, or if you are sleeping outdoors, use a mosquito net. Permethrin-treated mosquito nets offer enhanced protection compared to untreated ones. If you are bitten by mosquitoes, avoid scratching the bites to prevent further irritation or infection. Apply hydrocortisone cream or calamine lotion to alleviate itching. Over-the-counter antihistamine creams may also provide relief. For more information on managing mosquito bites, consult resources on symptoms and treatment.
